meta.rule: notes of 60 to 140 words, full sentences, written for the reader; no presenter direction, no everyday analogy

slides.title: Chapter 5: Wallet Recovery
slides.notes: This chapter explains how a Bitcoin wallet is recovered after a loss. A wallet does not hold coins; it holds keys, and the keys can be lost, so the chapter follows one seed from twelve recovery words to a whole tree of keys and to a backup that has been tested. The deck has 68 slides in seven parts, 27 code examples with their printed results and three true stories with real names and dates. The figure comes from Mastering Bitcoin, third edition, and every code example runs on the course page under Run slide code with the same library and the same data.

slides.title: Today's route through seven parts
slides.notes: The route has seven parts that follow the order of the chapter: keys in wallets, recovery codes, the BIP39 stack, the HD wallet, paths and descriptors, data that is not keys, and deploying and testing. Each row names the slides of its part, so a reader can jump straight to a part. The three counters give the size of the deck: 68 slides, 27 code examples with their results and three true stories. The last row covers the summary, the resources and the questions. A reader who finishes the deck should hold a backup that has been tested by a restore.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.notes: The seven questions are the questions of the chapter, written so that each one has its answer in a part of the deck. They begin with what a wallet contains and end with what must be backed up and how the backup is tested. In between they ask how a recovery code becomes a seed, how one seed makes a tree of keys, which recovery schemes exist, which derivation paths wallets use and where the book differs from the standards. The summary near the end returns to the same questions. A reader who can answer all seven without looking has understood the chapter.

slides.title: One chapter, eight branches
slides.notes: The chapter has eight branches, and the bars count the key concepts that the course page explains in each one. The hierarchical deterministic wallet has the most with 25, followed by derivation paths with 15, then the BIP39 stack and recovery codes with 14 each. Wallet keys has 10, backing up data that is not keys has 9, and the foundations and the deployment branch have 8 each. The seven parts of the deck follow these branches, every part opens with a divider, and each code slide shows the code, a note beside it and the printed result.

slides.title: Two guesses from 7,002 bitcoin
slides.notes: In 2011 Stefan Thomas, a programmer who had been technology chief at Ripple, was paid 7,002 bitcoin and kept the keys on an IronKey USB drive in a safe. He lost the paper with the password. On 12 January 2021 the reporter Nathaniel Popper told the story in the New York Times: eight of the ten allowed guesses were already used, and the drive locks for good after the tenth. Memory was his only backup. The lesson is that a recovery code tested in advance is the alternative to a password held in the head. The photograph shows Thomas in 2015.

slides.title: The tools we run today
slides.notes: Every code slide of this deck calls the same small Python library, which was written for reading and uses only the standard library. Its functions turn entropy into recovery words, words into a 512-bit seed, a seed into a master key, a parent into a child, a path into a key, a public key into a bc1q address, and a text into a descriptor checksum. Shamir splitting and the gap-limit scan are also included. The sample data table names the values that return on slide after slide: the book's 128 bits and twelve words, the BIP32 test seed, the BIP84 test code, a descriptor made by Bitcoin Core and the book's extended public key.

slides.title: Part 1: Keys in wallets
slides.notes: Part 1 asks what a wallet really holds. Six concepts are defined here: the wallet database, which is the file where a wallet keeps keys and notes; independent key generation, in which every key is made alone and needs its own backup; deterministic key generation, in which every key follows from one seed by a rule; the seed itself; the key tweak, a number added to a key to make a related key; and the hardware signing device, which signs without showing its keys. The diagram shows the central idea: one seed and one rule give key 0, key 1 and key 2, so a single backup covers them all.

slides.title: What a wallet really holds
slides.notes: A wallet is more than one program. The wallet application prepares a payment, the wallet database supplies the keys, a signing device signs, and the network receives the signed transaction. The four cards define the wallet database, a wallet that holds public keys only, external signing and the hardware signing device. A wallet with public keys only can see the funds sent to its keys and show them, but it cannot spend. External signing splits the work between one program that prepares the transaction and another program or device that signs it. Keys are the wallet; everything else can be rebuilt from them.

slides.title: Three ways to make keys
slides.notes: The book shows three ways to make keys. In the first, loose keys are made independently and each one needs its own backup. In the second, deterministic generation derives keys k0 to kn from one seed, so one backup is enough. In the third, hierarchical generation grows a tree of keys below the seed, which lets a wallet organise keys by purpose and account. The two figures come from Mastering Bitcoin, third edition. The difference matters for recovery: independent keys multiply the number of secrets to protect, while seed-based keys reduce the secrets to a single one.

slides.title: Concept guide for part 1
slides.notes: This table lists the concepts of part 1 together with the slides on which the deck shows each one and a short statement of what it means in the wallet. The wallet database is the file that stores keys and notes; independent key generation makes each key alone, so each needs its own backup; deterministic key generation means one seed and a rule always give the same keys. The seed is the one secret every key comes from, a key tweak is a number added to a key to make a related key, and a hardware signing device signs and never reveals its keys. The last two rows are the chapter itself and its technology stack.

slides.title: Code 1: Loose keys versus one seed
slides.notes: The code defines a seed and a rule that turns it into key number i by hashing the seed together with the index with SHA-256. It then asks the rule for keys 0, 1 and 2 and prints the first eight characters of each: aa74b609, 94af53de and fc092c45. Running the same lines again gives exactly the same keys, and the comparison prints True. This is the whole argument for deterministic wallets: one seed to back up, and every key follows from it. The example is code 1 of 27, and it runs on the course page under Run slide code with the chapter library.

slides.title: Part 2: Recovery codes
slides.notes: Part 2 asks how a seed is written down so that a human can keep it. Six concepts are defined: a recovery code, which is words or characters that stand for the seed; BIP39, which uses words from a list of 2,048 and a checksum; the rival schemes Electrum v2, Aezeed and Muun, which add versions, dates or encryption; SLIP39 and codex32, which split one secret into shares that can be recombined; the recovery code passphrase, an extra secret that changes the wallet; and the brainwallet, words chosen by the owner, which is not a recovery code. The diagram runs from entropy to a written code that is restored later.

slides.title: Six recovery code schemes
slides.notes: Six recovery code schemes are in use, and each adds something to the same goal. BIP39 uses words from a list of 2,048, a checksum and an optional passphrase. Electrum version 2 has no global word list and stores a version number inside the code. Aezeed, from the lnd wallet, adds two version numbers and a wallet birthday. Muun uses a non-word code that decrypts the keys in a separate document. SLIP39 splits one seed into several codes, for example five made and three needed. Codex32 lets shares be made and checked by hand with paper and a pen. The schemes differ in reliability, privacy and the ability to split.

slides.title: Why words, and what can go wrong
slides.notes: Words make a recovery code easy to remember, yet the book strongly urges writing it down, because memory fails. A brainwallet is made of words that the owner chose, whereas a recovery code is random and made by the wallet; chosen words are easy to guess. Coercion is a physical risk: someone who thinks you remember a code may force you to reveal it. The book cites over 100 attacks, and the 2026 copy of the list has 364 rows. A wallet birthday is a date stored in the code so that a restore need not scan the whole blockchain. The rule is to write it down, make it random and not depend on memory.

slides.title: Concept guide for part 2, schemes
slides.notes: This table lists the recovery schemes of part 2 with the slides that show them and what each one is. The recovery code is a set of words that stands for the seed, and BIP39 is the most common scheme. Electrum v2 has no global list and puts a version inside the code. Aezeed has versions and a wallet birthday, and Muun is a code that decrypts a separate document. SLIP39 gives shares of one seed with a threshold, and Codex32 gives shares and checksums made with paper and a pen. All seven answer the same question, how to write a seed down, with different trade-offs between reliability, privacy and splitting.

slides.title: Concept guide for part 2, choices
slides.notes: This table covers the choices that surround a recovery code. A passphrase is an extra secret mixed into the seed, so the same words with a different passphrase give a different wallet. Plausible deniability means a wallet that looks genuine and holds little, and a duress wallet is a decoy wallet opened by another passphrase and handed over under threat. A brainwallet is made of words the owner chose and is easy to guess. The wallet birthday is the creation date stored in the code. The last two rows are the book sections on seeds and recovery codes and on recovery code passphrases. If the passphrase is lost, the words alone open nothing.

slides.title: Code 2: Codes check themselves differently
slides.notes: Two schemes check themselves differently. The first line checks a codex32 string, which carries a long checksum over the whole text that can be verified by hand, and the run prints valid: True. Electrum marks a seed by the first digits of an HMAC, so the search tries seed 0, 1, 2 and so on until the HMAC begins with the digits 100. It stops at seed number 5483. BIP39, in contrast, takes its checksum bits from SHA-256, which a later slide shows. Every scheme has its own safety net, so a wallet can tell a mistyped code from a valid one. This is code 2 of 27.

slides.title: Code 3: Three of five shares recover the secret
slides.notes: The example is a small model of the idea behind SLIP39. A secret is split into five shares such that any three can rebuild it. The run combines shares 1, 2 and 3 and then shares 2, 3 and 4, and both groups give back the secret, printing True twice. Two shares, 1 and 2, give a wrong answer, and the run prints False. Two shares therefore reveal nothing about the secret, and three recover all of it. The model uses a polynomial over a prime field, which is the same principle that real share schemes apply. This is code 3 of 27 on the course page.

slides.title: Part 3: The BIP39 stack
slides.notes: Part 3 follows the BIP39 stack from random bits to a seed. Six concepts are defined: entropy, the random bits the code is made from; the checksum, a few bits that reveal a typo; the word list of 2,048 numbered words that everyone shares; the key-stretching function, repeated work that makes guessing slow; PBKDF2 with its salt, the stretcher BIP39 uses and the string it adds; and the root seed, the 512-bit result that starts the tree. The diagram shows the order: entropy, a checksum, eleven-bit pieces, words, the PBKDF2 stretch and the 512-bit seed.

slides.title: Twelve words between you and 128 bits
slides.notes: Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak of SatoshiLabs, the makers of Trezor, saw that nobody transcribes 128 raw bits correctly, and Aaron Voisine and Sean Bowe joined them. On 10 September 2013 they published BIP 39 in the public bips repository on GitHub, a way to write entropy as ordinary words. The recipe is 2,048 words of eleven bits each, a checksum folded in and key stretching from the words to the seed. The recovery code is therefore an interface standard between humans and entropy. The photograph shows Trezor One devices, and the link goes to the specification.

slides.title: Generating a recovery code
slides.notes: A recovery code is generated in five steps. First, make 128 bits of entropy for twelve words. Second, hash it with SHA-256. Third, append the first four bits of the hash as the checksum, which gives 132 bits. Fourth, split the 132 bits into twelve pieces of eleven bits. Fifth, look each piece up in the word list of 2,048 words. The arithmetic is twelve words times eleven bits, which equals 132 bits, which equals 128 bits of entropy plus 4 bits of checksum. Longer codes use more entropy: the book allows 128 to 256 bits, which gives 12 to 24 words.

slides.title: Code 4: A hash function changes half its bits
slides.notes: SHA-256 is the hash function inside BIP39, and this example shows its main property. Two inputs that differ by one letter, seed A and seed B, are hashed, and the two 256-bit results are combined with XOR so that every differing bit becomes a one. Counting the ones gives 126 of 256 bits, about half. A tiny change in the input therefore makes a huge difference in the output, which is why a checksum taken from a hash detects even a single mistyped word. This is code 4 of 27, and it uses only the hashlib module of the standard library.

slides.title: Code 5: How many words for how much entropy
slides.notes: BIP39 allows five sizes of entropy: 128, 160, 192, 224 and 256 bits. The loop turns an all-zero entropy of each size into a recovery code and counts the words. The counts are 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24, so each extra 32 bits adds three words. The result line shows the last pair, 256 bits and 24 words. More bits mean more words and a greater security strength, which is why a wallet that protects a large holding may choose 24 words, while 12 words from 128 bits is the usual default. This is code 5 of 27 on the course page.

slides.title: Code 6: From entropy to twelve words
slides.notes: The chapter's 128 bits of entropy, written as the hexadecimal string 0c1e24e5917779d297e14d45f14e1a1a, become its twelve words, and the comparison with the book's words prints True. Each word is a position in the BIP39 list, from 0 to 2047, and the table shows the twelve positions: 96, 1929, 459, 279, 956, 1866, 764, 333, 559, 1107, 1076 and 423. The first word, army, is position 96, which is the eleven bits 00001100000. Every word is therefore just an eleven-bit number. This is code 6 of 27, and the word list is read from the file that the library ships.

slides.title: Code 7: The checksum catches a wrong word
slides.notes: The first lines decode the recovery code back to entropy and print the entropy, 0c1e24e5917779d297e14d45f14e1a1a, together with True, which says that the last four bits match the checksum recomputed from the entropy. The second part changes the last word from crunch to army. The recomputed checksum no longer matches, so the check prints False and the decoded entropy is not trusted. A checksum turns a silent typo into a loud error. It cannot repair the typo, and it cannot catch every change, but it catches most. This is code 7 of 27 on the course page.

slides.title: Code 8: Text is normalised before stretching
slides.notes: The same word can be written in two ways: the letter e with an acute accent as one character, or an e followed by a combining accent. In the example the word cafe with an accent has 4 characters as typed and 5 after normalisation with the NFKD form. BIP39 requires the text to be normalised before stretching, so both spellings give the same seed, and the comparison prints True. Without this rule a wallet restored on another device could derive a different seed from the same visible words. This is code 8 of 27, and it uses the unicodedata module of the standard library.

slides.title: Code 9: PBKDF2 stretches the words with a salt
slides.notes: PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512 stretches the recovery words by repeating the work many times. The example hashes the same words with three settings and prints the first 12 hexadecimal digits: one round with the salt mnemonic gives d4a21305b044, 2048 rounds with the same salt give 5b56c417303f, and 2048 rounds with the salt mnemonic1 give 6b63963292ef. BIP39 uses 2048 rounds. The three results are unrelated, so a change of rounds or salt changes everything. The slowness is deliberate: each guess of a passphrase costs 2048 rounds. This is code 9 of 27 on the course page.

slides.title: Code 10: A passphrase opens a different wallet
slides.notes: A passphrase opens a different wallet. The example fixes one key path, m/84h/0h/0h/0/0, and defines a helper that derives the key from the words together with a passphrase and returns its address. With no passphrase the first address is bc1qg0azlj4w2lrq8jssrrz6eprt2fe7f7edm4vpd5; with the passphrase SuperDuperSecret it is bc1qp2dvcxvj4y5p5mesfgspljzdvnyzmqy2724n04. The twelve words are the same in both cases. The passphrase is therefore a second secret that must be backed up separately, and without it the words alone open the wrong wallet. This is code 10 of 27.

slides.title: Concept guide for part 3
slides.notes: This table lists the concepts of part 3 with the slides that show them. Entropy is the random bits a code is made from, the checksum is bits that reveal a typo, and the word list gives 2,048 words for eleven bits each. The key-stretching function is repeated hashing that makes guessing slow, PBKDF2 is the stretcher BIP39 uses with HMAC-SHA512, and the salt is a string that separates equal inputs. The root seed is the 512-bit seed that starts the tree. Together they describe how a recovery code becomes a seed, from entropy to the final 512 bits.

slides.title: Concept guide for part 3, book sections
slides.notes: The second table of part 3 lists the sections of the book. The section on BIP39 recovery codes is the standard that turns bits into words. Generating a recovery code covers entropy, checksum, eleven-bit pieces and words. From recovery code to seed covers stretching the words into a 512-bit seed. How much entropy you need covers the range of 128 to 256 bits, which is 12 to 24 words. The optional passphrase section explains the passphrase mixed into the salt. Each row names the slides where the deck shows the idea, so a reader can go from the section of the book to the code that runs.

slides.title: Part 4: The HD wallet
slides.notes: Part 4 grows a tree from one seed. Six concepts are defined: the master private key, the first private key of the tree; the master chain code, the 32 bytes that let the tree keep growing; child key derivation, a new key from a parent, a chain code and an index; hardened derivation, a step that only the private parent key can take; the extended key, a key and its chain code written as one string; and the index number, which picks the child, 0 to 2 to the power 31 minus 1 for normal children and above that for hardened ones. The diagram runs from the root seed through HMAC-SHA512 to the master key and extended keys.

slides.title: One seed, a tree of keys
slides.notes: The tree has a seed at the top and a master key, called m, below it. The master key has children m/0, m/1 and m/2, and each child has children of its own, such as m/0/0 and m/0/1, so every node is named by its path. Every node is a key and a chain code, 32 bytes each. The master is made by one HMAC of the seed. A child is made from its parent, the parent's chain code and an index. A backup of the seed therefore backs up the whole tree, because every node can be derived again from the root.

slides.title: Code 11: HMAC-SHA512 makes the master key
slides.notes: The example computes the master key from the BIP32 test seed. HMAC-SHA512 with the key Bitcoin seed gives 64 bytes, and the example splits them into two halves of 32 bytes. The left half is the master private key and the right half is the master chain code. The library function master does the same in one call, and the comparison prints True True. The printed key begins e8f32e723decf405 and has 64 hexadecimal digits. Half of the HMAC is the key and half is the chain code. This is code 11 of 27, and the diagram shows the seed of 16 bytes splitting into the two halves.

slides.title: Code 12: Child keys from a parent and an index
slides.notes: Child key derivation starts at the master pair and asks for children 0, 1 and 2. Each child receives its own private key and its own chain code, so the tree can keep growing. The table shows the first 12 hexadecimal digits: child 0 has the key 4e2cdcf2f14e and chain code d323f1be5af3, child 1 has 4df92b81d272 and 8dd96414ff4d, and child 2 has 271614f2ca44 and 6da671c6fba4. Three indexes give three unrelated children. The full values are 64 digits each. This is code 12 of 27 on the course page, and the chain code is what keeps the derivation unpredictable.

slides.title: Code 13: Hardened and normal children differ
slides.notes: Child number 0 lies in the normal range, below 2 to the power 31. Child number 2147483648 is the first hardened child and gives a different key from child 0, so the comparison prints False. In a path, the letter h adds 2 to the power 31 to the index, which the example confirms: the path m/0h has the single index 2147483648, which is the constant HARD, and the comparison prints True. The table lists the three cases. The letter h in a path is therefore a security decision, because hardened children cannot be derived from a public key. This is code 13 of 27 on the course page.

slides.title: Code 14: Why hardened steps protect the parent
slides.notes: A normal child private key, together with the parent's extended public key, exposes the parent private key. The example takes a parent key and its public key K, derives the normal child number 5, and then calls a function that works backwards: the extended public key plus one normal child private key, minus the hash value, gives the parent private key. The run prints True, which means the parent private key was recovered. A hardened step cannot be undone this way, because its hash is computed from the private key. This is why hardening protects the parent. The four boxes show the subtraction, and this is code 14 of 27.

slides.title: Code 15: Public keys derived without private keys
slides.notes: Public keys can be derived without private keys. The example derives child number 5 in two ways. Route one derives the private child and then computes its public key. Route two uses only the parent public key K and the chain code. Both routes end at the same public key, and the comparison prints True. This property lets a web shop make a fresh address for every customer while holding no private key at all, which slide 58 shows. It works only for normal children, because a hardened child needs the private parent key. This is code 15 of 27 on the course page.

slides.title: Code 16: Extended keys, xprv and xpub
slides.notes: An extended key is a key together with its chain code, written in Base58Check. The example serialises the master private key as an xprv and the master public key as an xpub; both are 111 characters long and begin with xprv and xpub. The fingerprint of the master key is 3442193e, four bytes that identify it, and the depth of the master key is 0 because it sits at the top of the tree. An xprv can spend and derive, while an xpub can only watch and derive public keys. This is code 16 of 27, and the table lists the four values that the run printed.

slides.title: Code 17: 2 to the 31 children, normal and hardened
slides.notes: The book writes 2,147,483,647 as the number of children of each kind, while BIP32 counts 2 to the power 31 for each kind. The example prints 2147483648, the value of HARD, and 2147483647, the last normal index. It then counts the two ranges: the normal indexes from 0 to 2^31 minus 1 and the hardened indexes from 2^31 to 2^32 minus 1 each hold 2147483648 children. The two kinds are equal in number. The book's figure is the last index, not the count. This is code 17 of 27, and it is one of the places where the book differs from the standard.

slides.title: Concept guide for part 4, the tree
slides.notes: This table lists the concepts of the tree in part 4 and the slides that show them. The master private key is the first private key of the tree, and the master chain code is the 32 bytes that let children be made. Child key derivation makes a new key from a parent key, a chain code and an index. The chain code is 32 bytes that keep derivation unpredictable, and the index number runs from 0 to 2^31 minus 1 for normal children, then hardened. Together they describe how one master pair produces every key of the wallet, with a numbered index choosing the child.

slides.title: Concept guide for part 4, extended keys
slides.notes: This table lists the extended keys of part 4. An extended key is a key plus its chain code in one string. The extended private key, xprv, can spend and derive. The extended public key, xpub, derives public keys only, so it can show every address of a wallet but cannot move funds. Hardened derivation is a step that needs the private parent key, which keeps a leaked xpub from exposing the private keys above it. The rule that follows is to give out the xpub when a program needs to watch or make addresses, and never to give out the xprv.

slides.title: Concept guide for part 4, book sections
slides.notes: The third table of part 4 lists the sections of the book. The section on hierarchical deterministic key generation, BIP32, describes one seed and a tree of keys. Creating an HD wallet from the seed gives the master key and chain code. Private child key derivation makes a child private key from the parent private key, and using derived child keys explains why hardened children never expose the parent. Extended keys are a key plus a chain code as xprv or xpub. Public child key derivation derives public keys from a public key, hardened child derivation needs the private parent key, and the last row covers index numbers: 0 to 2^31 minus 1 normal, 2^31 and up hardened.

slides.title: Part 5: Paths and descriptors
slides.notes: Part 5 asks which key is which and how to write it down. Six concepts are defined: the HD wallet path, the numbers from the master key down to one key; BIP43 and BIP44, in which the first number names the scheme and BIP44 fixes five levels; implicit paths, which a standard fixes and which therefore need not be recorded; explicit paths, written down next to the recovery code; output script descriptors, text that names the script and the keys behind it; and the key origin, the bracket that names a key's parent fingerprint and path. The diagram runs from the recovery code through a path and a descriptor to the addresses.

slides.title: Code 18: Reading a key path level by level
slides.notes: A path is a list of child numbers below the master key m. The example reads the path m/84h/0h/0h/1/7 into its numbers and labels them with the five levels that BIP43 and BIP44 define: purpose, coin, account, change and index. Printing each number together with whether it is hardened shows that the first three are hardened and the last two are normal, so the count of hardened levels is 3. The diagram marks the hardened levels in orange: purpose 84h, coin 0h and account 0h. Change is 1 and index is 7. This is code 18 of 27 on the course page.

slides.title: Code 19: Four standard paths, four address types
slides.notes: Four standard paths give four address types from one test recovery code. Purpose 44 gives a legacy pay-to-public-key-hash address, which starts with 1. Purpose 49 wraps a segwit script inside a script hash, which starts with 3. Purposes 84 and 86 give native segwit, which starts with bc1q, and taproot, which starts with bc1p. The table lists the first address of each, for example bc1qcr8te4kr609gcawutmrza0j4xv80jy8z306fyu for purpose 84. Each address follows from the same words and a different purpose number, which is why a backup must record which paths were used. This is code 19 of 27.

slides.title: Code 20: Our address equals the standard's own
slides.notes: The example derives the first address of the BIP84 test recovery code at the path m/84h/0h/0h/0/0 and compares it with the address that BIP84 publishes and that Bitcoin Core derives, bc1qcr8te4kr609gcawutmrza0j4xv80jy8z306fyu. The comparison prints True. The table shows the two sources side by side with the same address and an Equal row that reads True. Checking a library against a published test vector is how a reader knows that the derivation is correct before trusting it with real keys. The path here is written explicitly, which is the point of the slide. This is code 20 of 27.

slides.title: Code 21: A key tweak makes the taproot key
slides.notes: A key tweak turns a public key into a related key. The example derives the internal key of the BIP86 path and then computes the taproot output key by adding a number derived from a hash, multiplied by the generator point. The first 12 hexadecimal digits of the internal key are cc8a4bc64d89 and those of the output key are a60869f0dbcf. The taproot address encodes the tweaked key, not the internal one, and it begins bc1p5cyxnuxmeuwuvkwfem96lqzszd02n6xd. Adding a number to a key gives a related key, and that is the whole idea of the tweak. This is code 21 of 27.

slides.title: Implicit and explicit paths
slides.notes: Paths are either implicit or explicit. An implicit path is fixed by a standard such as BIP44, so the wallet does not record it. An explicit path is written down with the recovery code, usually in descriptor notation. The table lists the four purposes as the book gives them: 44 for BIP44 with the path m/44'/0'/0' for legacy scripts, 49 for BIP49 with m/49'/1'/0' where coin type 1 is testnet in SLIP-0044, 84 for BIP84 with m/84'/0'/0' for native segwit, and 86 for BIP86 with m/86'/0'/0' for single-key taproot. Know which paths are implicit and write down the rest.

slides.title: Code 22: A descriptor with its checksum and origin
slides.notes: An output script descriptor is one line of text that names the script and the keys behind it. The example prints the last eight characters of the checksum of the descriptor that Bitcoin Core made, afwvtk2s, which BIP380 appends after the hash sign. It then parses the key origin in the bracket at the start, which gives the parent fingerprint 73c5da0a and a hardened path: all three steps are True. Finally it builds a two-of-three multisignature descriptor, wsh(multi(2,A,B,C)), and its own checksum ends uhe03042. One line of text can rebuild the structure of a wallet. This is code 22 of 27.

slides.title: Multisignature, multipath and miniscript
slides.notes: Descriptors grow in three ways. A multisignature descriptor lists several keys and requires signatures from at least a threshold of them: in the diagram keys A, B and C sit inside wsh(multi(2,A,B,C)), and any two may sign. A multipath descriptor holds a tuple in one path step, such as the receiving and the change branch, in a single descriptor. Miniscript is a language for a subset of scripts that supports analysis and generic signing. In each case the descriptor keeps the rules of the wallet in one line of text that can be saved with the backup.

slides.title: Concept guide for part 5
slides.notes: This table lists the concepts of part 5 with the slides that show them. The HD wallet path is a list of numbers from the master key to one key. BIP43 sets the purpose number below the master key, and BIP44 fixes five levels: purpose, coin, account, change and index. Implicit paths are fixed by a standard and not recorded, whereas explicit paths are written down with the backup. Output script descriptors are text that names the script and the keys. A path names exactly one key, and a descriptor names the whole structure of a wallet, so a backup needs one or the other.

slides.title: Concept guide for part 5, book sections
slides.notes: The second table of part 5 lists the sections of the book. The section on backing up key derivation paths says that paths or descriptors must be saved with the recovery code. The HD wallet key identifier is the path, and m/84h/0h/0h/0/0 names exactly one key. Navigating the HD wallet tree structure means following the levels purpose, coin, account, change and index. If the path is not written down with the key, a restored wallet may derive from the wrong path and show an empty balance, even though every word of the code is right.

slides.title: Part 6: Data that is not keys
slides.notes: Part 6 shows that a recovery code is not the whole backup. Six concepts are defined: a label, a note that names an address or a transaction; BIP329, a standard file format for exporting labels; the Lightning Network, which makes payments off the blockchain with their own state; static channel backups, a one-time backup that helps recover channel funds; encryption, which turns readable data into data that only a key holder reads; and the encrypted wallet backup, the whole database encrypted by a key from the seed. The diagram runs from the keys from the seed to labels, protocol data and an encrypted backup.

slides.title: Code 23: Labels exported in the BIP329 format
slides.notes: A label is a note that names an address or a transaction, and it is not derived from the seed. BIP329 writes one JSON object per line, so any program can read the backup. The example builds two rows, one address labelled rent and one transaction labelled pay, and prints each as a JSON line; the table shows the type, the first characters of the reference and the label. Two rows are exported, which the result line confirms. Labels are data too, and a restored wallet that shows the right balance but no descriptions has lost them. This is code 23 of 27 on the course page.

slides.title: Channels and encrypted backups
slides.notes: Two answers exist for data that the keys cannot rebuild. A static channel backup is saved once when a channel opens; if data is lost, the backup helps close the channel, but it cannot guarantee a result. An encrypted wallet backup holds the whole wallet database, with keys, labels and protocol data, and is made often and automatically. It is encrypted with a key derived from the seed, stored as a copy, and decrypted by the seed at restore time. The rule is that keys come back from the seed and everything else needs its own copy.

slides.title: The 200,000 BTC in a forgotten wallet file
slides.notes: On 21 March 2014, three weeks after the bankruptcy filing, Mark Karpeles, chief executive of Mt. Gox, said the exchange had found about 200,000 BTC. Simon Sharwood of The Register reported it. The coins sat in an old-format wallet file that the company believed was empty and had never checked. A file made by software two generations older still held spendable keys. Wallet files hold keys for as long as they exist, so a file should be labelled and tested and never discarded blindly. The picture is the Mt. Gox logo, in the public domain, and the link goes to the report.

slides.title: Part 7: Deploying and testing
slides.notes: Part 7 puts keys to work and tests the backup. Six concepts are defined: extended public key deployment, an xpub placed where it makes addresses; the payment processor, software that turns an xpub into a working shop; the gap limit, how many unused addresses in a row a scan checks; cold storage, keys kept where no connected computer can read them; the written backup, the recovery code on a physical medium; and testing a backup, a restore drill before it is needed. The diagram shows the order: the xpub on the shop, a customer paying, keys staying cold and a restore drill.

slides.title: Code 24: A web shop that holds no private key
slides.notes: A web shop can accept payments without holding any private key. The example parses the book's extended public key, decompresses its key, and derives public children 0, 1 and 2 with the chain code. For each customer it prints a fresh address: bc1qv32edz2zpvhmmjkd7vq2wcnhacys0pku9vh5jw, bc1qtqvqy3kyl5y6dmvk65p7e966k8ycyhwg9ypw3p and bc1qw399x6vyt7jhurm7h3ylc0uldlqr7wj9clk5ng. No private key exists on the server, so a break-in cannot steal the funds. Publish the xpub, and the keys never touch the internet. This is code 24 of 27 on the course page.

slides.title: Code 25: The gap limit decides how far a scan looks
slides.notes: The gap limit decides how far a scan looks. In the example a wallet received payments on keys 0, 3 and 25. The scan stops after a number of unused keys in a row, and the example tries gaps of 5, 10, 20 and 30. Gaps below 22 miss key 25, because there are 21 unused keys between key 3 and key 25, so only the gap of 30 reaches it and finds all three keys. A scan that stops too early misses money that is still in the wallet. This is why a restore may need a larger gap. This is code 25 of 27.

slides.title: Code 26: A digital signature fails if the message changes
slides.notes: A digital signature binds one key to one message. The example fixes a toy private key and its public key, hashes the message pay 1 and signs the hash. The signature verifies for that message and prints True. It fails for any other message, such as pay 2, and prints False. The nonce in the example is fixed to keep the run repeatable; a real wallet must never choose it by hand. This is the property that lets a hardware signing device sign a transaction without revealing its key: anyone can verify, and nobody without the key can sign. This is code 26 of 27.

slides.title: Cold storage and the hardware signing device
slides.notes: Cold storage means keys created and stored offline, which the book advises for any significant holding. The diagram shows the flow: a wallet on a connected computer holds only public keys and prepares an unsigned transaction, the offline signing device signs it, and the signed transaction returns for broadcast. A hardware signing device signs transactions and never shows the private keys. The written backup is the recovery code on paper or metal, stored apart from the device. Together they give offline keys, a device that signs and a code on paper, and a thief would need all three places.

slides.title: Code 27: The restore drill, a typo opens another wallet
slides.notes: The restore drill tests whether a backup works. The example defines a helper that derives the first address of a recovery code at the path m/84h/0h/0h/0/0, and the address of the BIP84 test code is written down as noted when the wallet is created. Restoring from the right code gives the same address, so the first comparison prints True. Changing one word, about to above, gives a different wallet, and the second comparison prints False. A single wrong word therefore opens another, empty wallet with no error. Test the restore, not your luck. This is code 27 of 27 on the course page.

slides.title: What a complete backup holds
slides.notes: A complete backup holds five things: the recovery code, the passphrase if one is used, the paths or descriptors, the public keys of other signers in a multisignature wallet, and the labels and protocol data. After the five items comes the test: restore from the backup alone and check the first address. The closing remark says that data loss is nobody's fault but cannot be reversed, so the holder makes the backups and tests them. A backup is complete only when a restore drill succeeds, because only a restore shows that nothing is missing.

slides.title: Concept guide for parts 6 and 7
slides.notes: The last table lists the concepts of parts 6 and 7 with the slides that show them. A label is text naming an address or a transaction, and BIP329 stores one JSON line per label. A static channel backup helps recover channel funds but gives no guarantee. The gap limit is how many unused addresses in a row a scan checks, and the section called Mind the Gap explains it. Backing up nonkey data keeps labels and protocol data apart from the seed, and an extended public key on a web store lets the shop make a fresh address for each customer without any private key.

slides.title: Check yourself against the code slides
slides.notes: Six questions test the chapter, and the table names the code slide that answers each one. Why is one seed better than many loose keys? Code 1. How many words does 256 bits of entropy make? Code 5. What does the checksum protect against? Code 7. Why does a passphrase change the wallet? Code 10. Why are account levels hardened? Code 14. How do you know a backup works? Code 27. A reader should answer each question without looking and then check the answer against the code slide and its printed result.

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.notes: The chapter in five lines: wallets stopped storing keys and started deriving them, so one seed is backed up once. A recovery code is entropy in words, eleven bits a word with the checksum included. Words become a 512-bit seed by deliberate slowness, and a passphrase forks the wallet. The HD tree gives every purpose a numbered key, and hardened steps protect the parent. Beyond keys come paths, labels, channels and a backup that counts only once it has been restored. Each line summarises one group of slides, and the code slides of that group carry the proof.

slides.notes: The resources are grouped by kind, and every entry is a live link. Standards: BIP 39 for mnemonic codes, BIP 32 for HD wallets, BIP 84 for P2WPKH derivation and BIP 380 for output script descriptors. The seminal work is the Bitcoin paper. The tools are Ian Coleman's BIP39 tool, to be used offline, and BTCPay Server. A tutorial, two community forums, the course repository and a video on BIP-39 words complete the list. The course page holds the same code.

slides.title: What you should now be able to say
slides.notes: After this chapter a reader should be able to say four things, each with its proof in the deck. Why one seed replaced bags of keys: code 1 shows that one seed gives every key again. What twelve words carry and how they become a tree: codes 6 to 12 show eleven-bit words, the stretch to 512 bits and the master key. Which path a wallet walks and who else can walk it: codes 18 to 22. What a tested backup is: code 27, where one wrong word opens another wallet. The slide closes the deck and invites questions.
